exampleAnswers.title: Calculating a Definite Integral of Function Using Substitution

question.explanation:
We start by changing the variable: \begin{align*} u &= 4x+1 \\[5pt] \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}&=4 \\[5pt] \textrm{d}u &=4\,\textrm{d}x \\[5pt] \dfrac{1}{4}\textrm{d}u &= \textrm{d}x \end{align*}

Next, we create a table for the limits of integration using the rule $u = 4x+1.$ \[ \begin{array}{|c|c|} \hline x& 0& 2\\ \hline u& 1& 9\\ \hline \end{array} \]

So, the integral in terms of the new variable is \[ \int_{0}^{2} \sqrt{\left(4x+1 \right)^{3}}\, \textrm{d}x =\int_{1}^{9} \sqrt{u^{3}}\,\cdot \dfrac{1}{4}\, \textrm{d}u. \]

Finally, we can solve it and get \[ \eqalign{ \int_{1}^{9} \sqrt{u^{3}}\,\cdot \dfrac{1}{4}\, \textrm{d}u &=\dfrac{1}{4}\int_{1}^{9} u^{3/2}\, \textrm{d}u\\[5pt] &=\dfrac{1}{4}\cdot\left.\dfrac{2}{5}u^{5/2}\right|_{1}^{9}\\[5pt] &=\dfrac{1}{4}\cdot\dfrac{2}{5}\left(9^{5/2}-1^{5/2}\right)\\[5pt] &=\dfrac{1}{10}\left((3^2)^{5/2}-1\right)\\[5pt] &=\dfrac{1}{10}\left(3^5-1\right)\\[5pt] &=\dfrac{1}{10}\left(243-1\right)\\[5pt] &=\dfrac{242}{10}\\[5pt] &=\dfrac{121}{5}. } \]

question.explanation:
We start by changing the variable: \begin{align*} u &= 2x-1 \\[5pt] \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}&=2 \\[5pt] \textrm{d}u &=2\,\textrm{d}x \\[5pt] \dfrac{1}{2}\textrm{d}u &= \textrm{d}x \end{align*}

Next, we create a table for the limits of integration using the rule $u=2x-1.$ \[ \begin{array}{|c|c|} \hline x& 1& 2\\ \hline u& 1& 3\\ \hline \end{array} \]

So, the integral in terms of the new variable is \[ \int_{1}^{2} \sqrt{2x-1 }\, \textrm{d}x =\int_{1}^{3} \sqrt{u} \cdot \dfrac{1}{2}\textrm{d}u. \]

Finally, we can solve it and get

\[ \eqalign{ \int_{1}^{3} \sqrt{u} \cdot \dfrac{1}{2}\textrm{d}u &=\dfrac{1}{2}\int_{1}^{3} u^{1/2}\, \textrm{d}u\\[5pt] &=\dfrac{1}{2}\left.\cdot\dfrac{2}{3}u^{3/2}\right|_{1}^{3}\\[5pt] &=\dfrac{1}{2}\cdot \dfrac 23\left(3^{3/2}-1^{3/2}\right)\\[5pt] &=\dfrac{1}{3}\left((3^3)^{1/2}-1\right)\\[5pt] &=\dfrac{1}{3}\left(3\sqrt{3}-1\right)\\[5pt] &=\sqrt 3 - \dfrac 1 3. } \]

question.text: Compute the exact value of the definite integral.
question.explanation:
We start by changing the variable: \begin{align*} u &= x^2+1 \\[5pt] \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}&=2x \\[5pt] \textrm{d}u &=2x\,\textrm{d}x \end{align*}

Next, we create a table for the limits of integration using the rule $u = x^2+1.$ \[ \begin{array}{|c|c|} \hline x& 0& \sqrt{3}\\ \hline u& 1& 4\\ \hline \end{array} \]

So, the integral in terms of the new variable is \[ \int_{0}^{\sqrt{3}} \sqrt{\left(x^2+1 \right)^{3}}\cdot 2x\, \textrm{d}x = \int_1^4 \sqrt{u^3}\,\textrm{d}u. \]

Finally, we can solve it and get \[ \eqalign{ \int_{1}^{4} \sqrt{u^3}\, \textrm{d}u &= \int_{1}^{4} u^{3/2}\, \textrm{d}u\\[5pt] &= \left.\dfrac{2}{5}u^{5/2}\right|_{1}^{4}\\[5pt] &= \dfrac{2}{5}\Big(4^{5/2}-1^{5/2}\Big)\\[5pt] &= \dfrac{2}{5}\left( (2^2)^{5/2}-1\right)\\[5pt] &= \dfrac{2}{5}\left(2^5-1\right)\\[5pt] &=\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid gainsboro]{\dfrac{62}{5}}. } \]

example.title: Calculating a Definite Integral of Function Using Substitution

question.explanation:
We start by changing the variable: \begin{align*} u &= 2x+1 \\[5pt] \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x} &= 2 \\[5pt] \textrm{d}u &= 2\,\textrm{d}x \\[5pt] \dfrac{1}{2}\textrm{d}u &= \textrm{d}x \end{align*}

Next, we create a table for the limits of integration using the rule $u = 2x+1.$ \[ \begin{array}{|c|c|} \hline x& 1& 2\\[5pt] \hline u& 3& 5\\[5pt] \hline \end{array} \]

So, the integral in terms of the new variable is \[ \int_1^2 \left(2x+1 \right)^{2}\, \textrm{d}x =\int_{3}^{5} u^{2}\cdot \dfrac{1}{2} \textrm{d}u. \]

Finally, we can solve it and get \[ \eqalign{ \int_{3}^{5} u^{2}\cdot \dfrac{1}{2} \textrm{d}u &=\dfrac{1}{2}\int_{3}^{5} u^{2}\, \textrm{d}u\\[5pt] &=\dfrac{1}{2}\left.\cdot\dfrac{1}{3}u^{3}\right|_{3}^{5}\\[5pt] &=\dfrac{1}{2}\cdot \dfrac{5^{3}-3^{3}}{3}\\[5pt] &=\dfrac{1}{2}\cdot \dfrac{125-27}{3}\\[5pt] &=\dfrac{98}{6}\\[5pt] &=\dfrac{49}{3}. } \]

example.title: Calculating a Definite Integral of Function Using Substitution

question.explanation:
We start by changing the variable: \begin{align*} u &= 3x+1 \\[5pt] \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x} &= 3 \\[5pt] \textrm{d}u &= 3\,\textrm{d}x \\[5pt] \dfrac{1}{3}\textrm{d}u &= \textrm{d}x \end{align*}

Next, we create a table for the limits of integration using the rule $u = 3x+1.$ \[ \begin{array}{|c|c|} \hline x& 0& 1\\ \hline u& 1& 4\\ \hline \end{array} \]

So, the integral in terms of the new variable is \[ \int_0^1 \sqrt{\left(3x+1 \right)^3}\,\textrm{d}x =\int_1^4 \sqrt{u^3} \cdot \dfrac{1}{3} \textrm{d}u. \]

Finally, we can solve it and get \[ \eqalign{ \int_{1}^{4} \sqrt{u^3}\cdot\dfrac{1}{3} \textrm{d}u &=\dfrac{1}{3}\int_{1}^{4} u^{3/2}\, \textrm{d}u\\[5pt] &=\dfrac{1}{3}\cdot\left.\dfrac{2}{5}u^{5/2}\right|_{1}^{4}\\[5pt] &=\dfrac{1}{3}\cdot\dfrac{2}{5}\left(4^{5/2}-1^{5/2}\right)\\[5pt] &=\dfrac{2}{15}\left((2^2)^{5/2}-1\right)\\[5pt] &=\dfrac{2}{15}\left(2^5-1\right)\\[5pt] &=\dfrac{2}{15}\left(32-1\right)\\[5pt] &=\dfrac{62}{15}. } \]

exampleAnswers.title: Calculating a Definite Integral of a Rational Function Using Substitution

question.explanation:
We start by changing the variable: \begin{align*} u &= x^4+9 \\[5pt] \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x} &= 4x^3 \\[5pt] \textrm{d}u &= 4x^3\,\textrm{d}x \\[5pt] \dfrac{1}{4}\textrm{d}u &= x^3\,\textrm{d}x \end{align*}

Next, we create a table for the limits of integration using the rule $u = x^4+9.$ \[ \begin{array}{|c|c|} \hline x& 0& 2\\ \hline u& 9& 25\\ \hline \end{array} \]

So, the integral in terms of the new variable is \[ \int_{0}^{2} \dfrac{1}{(x^4+9)}\,x^3 \,\textrm{d}x = \int_{9}^{25} \dfrac{1}{u}\cdot \dfrac{1}{4} \textrm{d}u. \]

Finally, we can solve it and get

\[ \eqalign{ \int_{9}^{25} \dfrac{1}{u}\cdot \dfrac{1}{4} \textrm{d}u &=\dfrac{1}{4}\int_{9}^{25} \dfrac{1}{u}\, \textrm{d}u\\[5pt] &=\dfrac{1}{4}\Big.\ln(u)\Big|_{9}^{25}\\[5pt] &=\dfrac{1}{4}(\ln(25)-\ln (9))\\[5pt] &=\dfrac{1}{4}\left(\ln(5^2) -\ln(3^2)\right)\\[5pt] &=\dfrac{1}{4}\left(2\ln(5) - 2\ln(3)\right)\\[5pt] &=\dfrac{1}{4}\cdot2\left(\ln(5) - \ln(3)\right)\\[5pt] &=\dfrac{1}{2}\ln\left(\dfrac53\right). } \]

example.title: Calculating a Definite Integral of a Rational Function Using Substitution

question.explanation:
We start by changing the variable: \begin{align*} u &= x^3+2 \\[5pt] \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x} &= 3x^2 \\[5pt] \textrm{d}u &= 3x^2\,\textrm{d}x\\[5pt] \dfrac{1}{3}\textrm{d}u &= x^2\,\textrm{d}x \end{align*}

Next, we create a table for the limits of integration using the rule $u = x^3+2.$ \[ \begin{array}{|c|c|} \hline x& -1& 1\\ \hline u& 1& 3\\ \hline \end{array} \]

So, the integral in terms of the new variable is \[ \int_{-1}^{1} \dfrac{1}{(x^3+2)}\, x^2 \,\textrm{d}x = \int_{1}^{3} \dfrac{1}{u}\cdot \dfrac{1}{3}\textrm{d}u. \]

Finally, we can solve it and get

\[ \eqalign{ \int_{1}^{3} \dfrac{1}{u}\cdot \dfrac{1}{3} \textrm{d}u &=\dfrac{1}{3}\int_{1}^{3} \dfrac{1}{u}\, \textrm{d}u\\[5pt] &=\dfrac{1}{3}\Big.\ln(u)\Bigg|_{1}^{3}\\[5pt] &=\dfrac{1}{3}(\ln(3)-\ln (1))\\[5pt] &=\dfrac{1}{3}\ln(3). } \]

example.title: Calculating a Definite Integral of a Rational Function Using Substitution

question.explanation:
We start by changing the variable: \begin{align*} u &= 2x^3+4 \\[5pt] \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x} &= 6x^2 \\[5pt] \textrm{d}u &= 6x^2 \,\textrm{d}x\\[5pt] \dfrac12\,\textrm{d}u &= 3x^2\,\textrm{d}x \end{align*}

Next, we create a table for the limits of integration using the rule $u=2x^3+4.$ \[ \begin{array}{|c|c|} \hline x& 1& 2\\ \hline u& 6&20\\ \hline \end{array} \]

So, the integral in terms of the new variable is \[ \int_1^2 \dfrac{1}{2x^3+4} \cdot 3 x^2\,\textrm{d}x = \int_6^{20} \dfrac{1}{u} \cdot \dfrac12\,\textrm{d}u. \]

Finally, we can solve it and get \[ \eqalign{ \int_6^{20} \dfrac{1}{u}\cdot \dfrac12 \,\textrm{d}u &= \dfrac12\int_{6}^{20} \dfrac{1}{u}\, \textrm{d}u\\[3pt] &= \dfrac12\Big.\ln (u)\Big|_{6}^{20}\\[3pt] &= \dfrac12\left(\ln (20) - \ln (6) \right)\\[3pt] &= \dfrac12\ln \left(\dfrac{20}{6}\right)\\[3pt] &= \dfrac12\ln \left(\dfrac{10}{3}\right). } \]

example.title: Calculating a Definite Integral of a Rational Function Using Substitution

question.explanation:
We start by changing the variable: \begin{align*} u &= x^2 + 1 \\[5pt] \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x} &= 2x \\[5pt] \textrm{d}u &= 2x \,\textrm{d}x\\[5pt] \dfrac{1}{2}\textrm{d}u &= x\,\textrm{d}x \end{align*}

Next, we create a table for the limits of integration using the rule $u = x^2 + 1.$ \[ \begin{array}{|c|c|} \hline x& 0& 1\\ \hline u& 1& 2\\ \hline \end{array} \]

So, the integral in terms of the new variable is \[ \int_{0}^{1} \dfrac{1}{(x^2+1)} \,x \, \textrm{d}x = \int_{1}^{2} \dfrac{1}{u}\cdot \dfrac{1}{2}\, \textrm{d}u. \]

Finally, we can solve it and get

\[ \eqalign{ \int_{1}^{2} \dfrac{1}{u}\cdot \dfrac{1}{2}\, \textrm{d}u &=\dfrac{1}{2}\int_{1}^{2} \dfrac{1}{u}\, \textrm{d}u\\[5pt] &=\dfrac{1}{2}\Big.\ln (u)\Bigg|_{1}^{2}\\[5pt] &=\dfrac{1}{2}\left(\ln(2)-\ln (1)\right)\\[5pt] &=\dfrac{1}{2}\ln(2). } \]

question.text: Compute the exact value of the definite integral.
question.explanation:
First, notice that we can express our integral as \begin{eqnarray} \eqalign{ \int_0^{\sqrt3} \dfrac {x+1}{x^2+1}\, \textrm{d}x &= \int_0^{\sqrt3} \dfrac {x}{x^2+1}\, \textrm{d}x + \int_0^{\sqrt3} \dfrac {1}{x^2+1}\, \textrm{d}x. } \end{eqnarray}

To evaluate the first integral, we start by changing the variable: \begin{align*} u &= x^2 + 1 \\[5pt] \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x} &= 2x \\[5pt] \textrm{d}u &= 2x\,\textrm{d}x \\[5pt] \dfrac{1}{2}\textrm{d}u &= x\,\textrm{d}x \end{align*}

Next, we create a table for the limits of integration using the rule $u=x^2+1.$ \[ \begin{array}{|c|c|} \hline x& 0& \sqrt3\\ \hline u& 1& 4\\ \hline \end{array} \]

So, the first integral in terms of the new variable is \[ \int_0^{\sqrt3} \dfrac{1}{(x^2+1)}\, x\,\textrm{d}x = \int_1^4 \dfrac{1}{u}\cdot \dfrac{1}{2}\textrm{d}u. \]

To evaluate the second integral, we can use the definition of $\arctan x.$ Finally, we can solve the integral and get \[ \eqalign{ \int_0^{\sqrt3} \dfrac {x+1}{x^2+1}\, \textrm{d}x &= \int_1^4 \dfrac {1}{u}\cdot \dfrac{1}{2} \textrm{d}u + \int_0^{\sqrt3} \dfrac {1}{x^2+1}\, \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= \dfrac 12 \int_1^4 \dfrac {1}{u}\, \textrm{d}u + \arctan x\Bigg|_0^{\sqrt3} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac 12 \Big.\ln (u)\Bigg|_1^4 + \left(\dfrac{\pi}3 - 0\right) \\[5pt] &= \dfrac 12( \ln (4) - \ln (1)) + \dfrac{\pi}{3}\\[5pt] &= \dfrac 12 \ln (2^2) + \dfrac{\pi}{3}\\[5pt] &= \dfrac 12\cdot 2 \ln (2) + \dfrac{\pi}{3}\\[5pt] &=\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid gainsboro]{\ln(2) + \dfrac{\pi}{3}}. } \]
